evidence: Cic. Tusc. 1.16: nihil tē interpellābō, continentem ōrātiōnem audīre mālō (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: To break in on someone who is talking or at work. Canius wanted a little garden where he could enjoy himself sine interpellātōribus, with no one to disturb him (Cic. Off. 3.58). See also don’t interrupt me!

evidence: Cic. Mur. 35: diēs intermissus aut nox interposita saepe perturbat omnia (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of plans, order or a mind thrown into disorder (see confuse, shock), rather than of a person interrupted.

evidence: Cic. de Or. 2.3 (Lewis & Short, s.v. interveniō): verēns nē molestī vōbīs intervenīrēmus
terms.comment: The polite way to ask whether one is disturbing: Num molestus sum?

phrases.english: Don’t interrupt. Go on with what you were saying.

phrases.latin: tū vērō ut mē et appellēs et interpellēs et obloquāre et colloquāre velim. quid enim mihi suāvius?
phrases.english: I want you to call me, interrupt me, talk over me and talk with me. What could be sweeter?

phrases.latin: dictitābat sē hortulōs aliquōs emere velle, quō invītāre amīcōs et ubi sē oblectāre sine interpellātōribus posset
phrases.english: he kept saying he wanted to buy some little garden to invite his friends to, where he could enjoy himself undisturbed
